title: Emma Woodhouse Handles a Hostile Offboarding
context_md:
Emma Woodhouse, IAM Specialist at *Highbury Networks*, gets a 4:55 p.m. call from HR: a senior systems engineer named Frank Churchill is being terminated for cause, effective immediately. Frank has accounts in roughly forty systems — Highbury's on-prem Active Directory, two cloud tenants, the customer support tool, the source code repository, the secrets vault, and a dozen SaaS apps onboarded over the years through the company's identity provider.

Emma's nightmare: Highbury never finished cleaning up the IAM landscape after last year's acquisition, so some apps still use local accounts that were never wired to the IdP. Frank also held a long-lived API token for the deployment pipeline and has SSH keys cached on at least two laptops.

Emma needs to revoke access cleanly, prevent Frank from re-authenticating with cached credentials, ensure none of his automation accounts continue running with his identity attached, and produce an audit-ready record for legal. She also wants to use this incident to push leadership toward closing the structural gaps — federation coverage, secrets rotation, and a real PAM rollout — before the next termination.
prompt_md: Walk through Emma's offboarding playbook by selecting the correct option for each step.
body_md:
Emma's first action is to disable Frank's account at the **{{authority}}**, which acts as the single source of truth for any application connected via federation. For applications that remain SAML- or OIDC-federated, this single change effectively kills new sessions because each app trusts assertions issued by that source.

However, federated logout does not invalidate **{{cached_artifact}}** that may already be sitting in Frank's browser or device. To kill those, Emma triggers a global session/token revocation in the IdP and the SaaS apps that support it.

For the long-lived deployment-pipeline token, Emma must perform an immediate **{{secret_action}}** — and going forward, Highbury should adopt **{{secret_practice}}** so that no human-owned credential lives longer than the human's tenure.

The SSH keys cached on Frank's laptops are best handled by removing his public key from the **{{ssh_location}}** on every server he could reach. Long-term, Emma will route all SSH access through a **{{pam_tool}}**, which brokers session-by-session credentials and records keystrokes for high-privilege sessions.

For the local accounts on un-federated legacy apps, Emma must disable each one manually; this is a textbook failure of **{{lifecycle_gap}}**. To prevent recurrence, Emma will propose **{{provisioning_protocol}}**, the standard for automating provisioning and deprovisioning across SaaS.

Finally, to give legal a defensible timeline of every revocation action, Emma exports the **{{audit_artifact}}** from the IdP, PAM, and source repo.

authority.explanation: The IdP is the federated source of truth. Disabling the account there cuts off authentication for every SP that trusts it.

cached_artifact.explanation: Federation revokes the right to obtain *new* tokens but does not invalidate tokens already issued and cached client-side. Global sign-out / token revocation endpoints are needed to kill those.

secret_action.explanation: A compromised or orphaned long-lived secret must be rotated immediately — the old value revoked and any service that needs continued access reissued a new credential.

distractors: passwords printed and stored in a safe
permanent API keys committed to source control
static credentials emailed to each engineer
secret_practice.explanation: Modern secrets management issues short-lived credentials (minutes-to-hours) and rotates automatically, so that a leaked or orphaned secret has a tightly bounded blast radius.

ssh_location.explanation: A user's accepted public keys live in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on each server. known_hosts is the *client-side* list of trusted servers — different direction.

pam_tool.explanation: PAM brokers privileged sessions, vaults credentials, issues just-in-time access, and records sessions — exactly what Highbury needs for high-risk admin access.

lifecycle_gap.explanation: Identity lifecycle = provisioning, modification, *deprovisioning*. Apps with un-cleaned local accounts after a termination are a deprovisioning failure.

provisioning_protocol.explanation: SCIM is the standard for automating create/update/delete of user accounts across SaaS apps. SAML/OIDC handle authentication; SCIM handles the lifecycle plumbing.

audit_artifact.explanation: Access logs and audit trails (who, what, when, from where) are the legally defensible record that revocation actually occurred at a specific time.
